The CLI has no gate-edit path (task add rejects duplicate ids, task set ignores --gate), so correcting a gate means editing .genesis/project.json directly; that is safe because validateState checks only schema_version and policy, and gate evidence hashes are recomputed on each run.

knowledge.title: genesis checkpoint and index crash on this host via the Store Python alias
knowledge.text: graphizer.mjs spawns python3 to build the Python AST, then spawns git for the revision. On this machine python3 and python both resolve to the Microsoft Store App Execution Alias, which corrupts the Node process job-object state; the following git spawn dies natively with AssignProcessToJobObject (87), exit 3 / 0xC0000003. Minimal repro: spawnSync(python3, {input}) followed by spawnSync(git) in one Node process. Verified the real .venv/Scripts/python.exe does NOT trigger it, so the alias is the cause, and the base interpreter under C:/Program Files/WindowsApps is not directly executable. Consequence: genesis checkpoint, genesis index and genesis kickoff fail; gate, task, record, spec, plan and status all work. Fix is to disable the python.exe/python3.exe app execution aliases in Windows Settings, or install python.org Python. Not a blocker for building.

knowledge.title: Store Python alias crash is fixed by the venv, no Windows settings change needed
knowledge.text: Resolves the earlier AssignProcessToJobObject finding. A Windows venv ships python.exe and pythonw.exe but no python3.exe, so graphizer's spawnSync('python3') fell through to the Microsoft Store app execution alias. Copying .venv/Scripts/python.exe to .venv/Scripts/python3.exe and putting that directory first on PATH makes python3 resolve to the real interpreter; genesis checkpoint then succeeds and indexes 159 nodes with no warnings. Run genesis as: PATH="$PWD/.venv/Scripts:$PATH" node <kit>/tools/genesis.mjs <cmd> . -- or just activate the venv first. NOTE: .venv is gitignored, so python3.exe must be recreated after any fresh venv build; see requirements.txt header.

knowledge.title: Redaction must precede truncation, and dict.get needs a hashable key
knowledge.text: Two boundary bugs found in round 2 of L4 review, both in code written to fix round 1. (1) _error_text truncated a provider body to 300 chars and then replaced the credential, so a key straddling the cut survived as a recoverable 14-character fragment in a ModelError message that FR-10 persists. Redact the whole text first, truncate second. (2) _STOP_REASONS.get(choice.get('finish_reason')) assumed the value was hashable; a list or dict finish_reason raised TypeError: unhashable type, escaping the adapter and violating the invariant that only AgentSDKError subclasses leave ModelClient.send(). Using an unchecked value as a dict key is itself a shape assumption.

knowledge.title: Reviewer rotation found defects that reviewer effort did not
knowledge.text: M3 took five review rounds. Rounds 1-3 were one reviewer, which found exactly one boundary escape per round, all in the same region (the response parse path), each fix enumerating one more exception type. Round 4 swapped models and immediately found an escape in a region the first reviewer never examined: the totaliser's own error-message construction, where str(exc) runs inside the except block. Round 5, a third model running 20 hostile boundary probes and 39 mutants, found no escape at all. Conclusion for the remaining milestones: rotate the reviewer model between rounds rather than asking the same reviewer to look harder. A reviewer cannot find the defects its own mental model does not generate, and repeated rounds from one reviewer converge on its blind spots rather than on correctness.

knowledge.title: M5 must redact the chained __cause__ and traceback, not only the ModelError message
knowledge.text: Five rounds of redaction work covered the ModelError message text only. The adapter raises 'from exc', so the original provider exception is retained on __cause__ with its message unredacted, and the traceback holds frame locals. When M5 serialises RunEvent payloads (FR-10) or writes a RunFailed row, anything that walks __cause__, __context__ or formats a traceback bypasses every redaction built so far. This must be a stated requirement of the persistence layer, not a discovery in M5's review: the event writer redacts what it serialises, or it must refuse to serialise exception chains at all.

knowledge.title: Gate gaps hide as quality degradation, not failure
knowledge.text: The most valuable finding of M4's second review was not a defect but a gate gap: an assembler that forwarded only the last message survived all 222 tests. The existing tests checked that a tool message EXISTED in the request, and the assembler unit test used a single-message history, so nothing pinned full-history assembly. A run with truncated context does not fail -- it silently gets worse, which is the hardest failure mode to notice. Verified the gap by mutating the assembler (222 passed), added tests for full-history assembly and growing per-turn history, and re-verified the mutation is now caught (2 failures). Same treatment applied to RuntimeHook HALT and MODIFY at all four points, which were likewise unpinned. General lesson: when reviewing a gate, ask which mutations would degrade quality rather than break behaviour -- those are the ones tests forget.

knowledge.title: Concurrent appends are safe but not available; Phase 2 needs a retry or lock
knowledge.text: Measured, not assumed. PostgresSessionStore.append uses INSERT ... SELECT COALESCE(MAX(sequence_no),0)+1 inside one transaction. Under READ COMMITTED two concurrent transactions can read the same MAX. Probed with 12 barrier-synchronised writers on one run: 8 rows committed with unique contiguous sequence numbers 1..8, 0 duplicates, and 4 writers raised UniqueViolation. So SAFETY holds absolutely (no duplicate or reordered history can commit, guaranteed by UNIQUE (run_id, sequence_no)) while AVAILABILITY does not (a losing writer errors rather than serialising). Phase 0 has exactly one writer per run so this is unreachable today. Phase 2's concurrent subagents will need a retry-on-UniqueViolation loop or a per-run advisory lock; the safety property is pinned by a test so a future fix cannot regress it.

knowledge.title: Database tests can prove the database, not the code
knowledge.text: Against a real database a passing test often proves the DATABASE behaves rather than that the CODE is right. Two instances in M5: (1) CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS means mutating schema.sql cannot affect an already-created database, so schema assertions proved the live DB, not the file; (2) removing ORDER BY sequence_no survived every test because an append-only table returns rows in insertion order anyway. The fix in both cases is to make the environment stop cooperating: apply the schema into a throwaway namespace, and write rows out of order before asserting a read is ordered. Both were found by mutation, not by reading.

knowledge.title: Concurrent append: safety fixed, availability varies
knowledge.text: Re-measured after tenancy derivation changed the insert to a LEFT JOIN with GROUP BY. Three 12-writer trials: 0 duplicates and contiguous sequence numbers every time (safety unchanged), with 1, 1 and 0 UniqueViolation losers respectively -- previously a steady 4 of 12. Availability is timing-dependent and the failure mode is still reachable, so the Phase 2 retry-or-advisory-lock item stands; the earlier '4 of 12' figure should not be quoted as a fixed property.

knowledge.title: Name what you can, then back it with a total check
knowledge.text: unstorable_reason has two layers: named checks (NUL, non-finite, depth) for a precise diagnosis, and a backstop that attempts the serialisation the store actually performs -- json.dumps(allow_nan=False, ensure_ascii=False).encode('utf-8'). Round 3 shipped only the named layer and round 4 found a lone UTF-16 surrogate walking past it: a truncated surrogate escape is a legal RFC-8259 decode, models emit truncated pairs, and both TEXT and JSONB refuse the result. The backstop catches the CLASS (anything the serialiser cannot express) rather than the instance, which also closed huge integers for free. Same structure as the ModelClient total boundary: specific guards for good messages, one total guard for correctness. Verified in BOTH directions against a live database -- astral emoji, 4-byte CJK and int(1e308) are still accepted, so the helper does not over-reject and fail runs that should work.

knowledge.title: Name a test after the invariant it pins
knowledge.text: A round-4 reviewer reported INVARIANT-3c123c38 (token_count must not swallow BaseException) as unpinned, having mutated it and seen the usage-related subset stay green. The mutation does turn the FULL suite red -- the test existed -- but it was named test_base_exception_from_a_hostile_int_still_propagates, so no 'pytest -k usage' or '-k token_count' selection could find it. Renamed to test_usage_token_count_lets_base_exception_propagate; all three selections now go red. A guard nobody can locate is one a reviewer reasonably concludes is missing, and reviewers work by subset selection.

knowledge.title: Over-rejection is a defect in the same class as under-rejection
knowledge.text: unstorable_reason capped nesting at depth 60 and called anything deeper unstorable. Postgres stores 900-deep JSON without complaint, so a model returning deeply nested tool arguments had its call refused over a limit that does not exist. Found by probing the database for the helper's false positives, not by review -- four review rounds had all hunted the other direction. Fix: the walk is iterative with a visited-id set instead of recursive with a depth cap, so it never guesses about depth; the serialiser decides, and it happens to agree with Postgres exactly (both stop at ~1000, the interpreter recursion limit). Walking iteratively also keeps the named checks looking at any depth: deferring on depth would have stopped finding a NUL buried 300 levels down, which the backstop cannot catch because JSON escapes NUL happily.

knowledge.title: Overlapping guards need a test at each layer
knowledge.text: Two mutations survived the round-6 matrix because the storability guards overlap: removing ModelResponse's field walk still passed end-to-end, since _json_safe marks the same value downstream, and vice versa. Overlap is deliberate defence in depth, but an end-to-end test cannot pin either layer -- it only proves that at least one still works. Each layer now has a test at its own level (ModelResponse asserted directly on the type; _json_safe asserted on both its string and its str()-fallback branch). Where a mutation survives because another layer covers it, the answer is a narrower test, not a weaker claim.

knowledge.title: An exemption in the test is the tell
knowledge.text: Round 6 found ToolCall.__post_init__ exempting arguments_error from the field walk introduced in round 5 to end exemptions -- and the test asserting 'the guarantee is structural, not a list of names' contained 'if name == arguments_error: continue'. The fix and its guard were written together and the guard was shaped around the gap, so the suite could never have caught it. When a test carries a special case for the code under test, treat the special case as the finding, not as scaffolding: verify the exemption is load-bearing by deleting it and running the suite. Here it was not -- 380 tests passed with it gone.

knowledge.title: Two guards for one property hide each other
knowledge.text: Second occurrence in two rounds. The round-6 fix added BOTH a field-walk covering arguments_error and a follow-up check on the generated reason string; reintroducing the carve-out then left all 380 tests green, because whichever guard was removed the other still produced a storable value. The second guard was also unreachable -- the reason string is built from field names and our own messages, always ASCII. Resolution: keep the structural guard, delete the unreachable one. Where two guards enforce the SAME property rather than different ones, the redundancy does not add defence; it removes the suite's ability to notice either one being deleted. Compare KNOWLEDGE-fd4720a4, where the layers guarded genuinely different surfaces and the answer was a test per layer.

knowledge.title: Implementing a caveat's list is not implementing the caveat
knowledge.text: Round 6's caveat (c) read 'tenant_id, project_id, agent_spec_id and model_id are unchecked for storability'. The repair implemented exactly those four names, and round 7 rejected on principal_context -- the fifth caller-supplied value, which the caveat had not enumerated. A review names examples; the finding is the class. Read every caveat as 'what is the property, and where else does it fail?' rather than as a checklist. Same failure mode as rounds 5 and 6 (a check applied to the fields someone thought of), arriving this time through the review process itself rather than through the code.

knowledge.title: Test that a guard is RIGHT, not that it runs
knowledge.text: Rounds 5-7 were all 'the guard was not applied to X'. Round 8 was different and worse: the guard was applied, named, and tested -- and answered the wrong question. max_turns was validated with unstorable_reason, a JSON serialisability predicate, while runs.max_turns is INTEGER, so 2**31 passed the guard and failed at the write. The round-7 test asserted only that each parameter name appeared in a set of checked names, which a check returning the wrong answer passes trivially. Removing the max_turns check entirely left all 389 tests green. Coverage tests answer 'does a check run'; fitness tests answer 'does it refuse what the column refuses'. Only the second kind can fail. The replacement drives a genuinely unfit value through every parameter and requires a refusal.

knowledge.title: A carve-out copied between layers loses its reason
knowledge.text: column_rejection_reason excluded bools from the INTEGER range check with . That exclusion was copied from token_count, where it is right (a flag is not a token count) -- but in a column check its effect is the opposite: psycopg adapts a bool to SQL boolean, so True reaches an integer column as DatatypeMismatch after completing happily in memory. The exclusion looked harmless because True is trivially inside the int32 range, which is answering a different question again. When moving a guard between layers, re-derive why each exception exists rather than carrying it across.

knowledge.title: A mutation that proves a leak test must not write the real secret
knowledge.text: While mutation-testing M6's AC-10 assertion I mutated api.py to copy MODEL_API_KEY into runs.agent_spec_id. It worked -- the test caught it -- but the five rows outlived the mutation by the length of the restore, so a real credential sat in the database until the next gate run found it. Remediated by redacting the column in place (pinned to the key pattern, the test tenants and today's date), verified zero rows anywhere afterwards. The mutation now writes LEAK-CANARY-<first four chars>, which proves the value came from the key without the row ever holding it, and the AC-10 test scans for the canary as well so the mutation is still detectable. The harness also clears its own canary rows, because debris that fails a credential gate looks exactly like a real leak to whoever runs it next. General rule: a destructive mutation must be as reversible as the restore that follows it.

knowledge.title: Live models cannot be prompted into a validation failure
knowledge.text: AC-3 needs a malformed tool argument. Asked to call echo with the number 42, openai.gpt-4o-mini sends 42 and trips ToolValidationError, while bedrock.anthropic.claude-haiku-4-5 coerces it to the string 42 and validates cleanly -- measured twice per provider. Providers increasingly enforce the declared schema server-side, so a malformed argument from a compliant provider is rare, which is exactly why the SDK's validate step exists as defence rather than as a formality. Consequence for the golden eval: AC-1 and AC-2 are asserted on the live path (both providers reliably call the denied tool when instructed), AC-3 is asserted on a scripted run where the malformed call is guaranteed. An assertion that depends on which model happens to be strict is a flaky gate.

knowledge.title: Measure the class, not the one shape you tried
knowledge.text: M6 round 1 was rejected for not exercising AC-3 live, and my justification was that a validation failure cannot be driven by prompting -- measured twice per provider. The measurement was real but it covered ONE shape: a number where a string is declared, which openai rejects and claude coerces. The reviewer tested a different shape, a maxLength 8 constraint the instructed input cannot satisfy, and got ToolValidationError on both providers 4 runs out of 4 with the implementation never invoked. Reproduced here before believing it. A measurement justifying a design decision must cover the CLASS the decision is about, and the decision should name which shapes were tried. Same error as the guard defects in M5: generalising from the instance in front of me.

knowledge.title: Assert the property the criterion names, not something adjacent
knowledge.text: The M6 reviewer found four tests, all passing, each asserting one step removed from its claim: AC-10 said 'no credential in any row' but scanned an enumerated column subset (it missed a canary in run_events.tool_call_id on 120 rows); AC-2 said 'surfaced to the model' but read the persisted history; NFR-4 said 'no credential in model context' but inspected the ModelRequest object rather than the wire body; NFR-7 said principal_context is never read but asserted an error type rather than the decision. In every case the SDK was correct, so these were gate defects -- tests passing for reasons weaker than the claims they underwrite. Fixes: whole-row scans over every table via {table}::text, assertions on the next request actually sent, a recording httpx transport for the wire body, and identical decisions across three different principals. When writing a test, say the criterion out loud and check the assertion is about that noun.

knowledge.title: Mutation debris makes later mutations look killed
knowledge.text: Re-running the M6 matrix, the first mutation wrote a canary into run_events.tool_call_id. My cleanup script only knew about runs.agent_spec_id, so 162 rows survived -- and then failed the AC-10 test on every SUBSEQUENT mutation, making all of them look killed by it. The matrix was worthless in a way that reads as success. Fixed by cleaning between mutations, not after the batch, and by making the cleanup find the canary in any column of any table rather than the one column that leaked first. Third distinct way this project has produced a meaningless mutation result: a SQL-error mutant counted as a kill, an unrecognised pytest flag exiting 4, and now cross-contamination. Check WHICH test killed each mutant, not just that something did.

knowledge.title: Converting one proxy assertion does not convert its siblings
knowledge.text: M6 round 1 replaced four assertions that were one step removed from their claims. Round 2 found the identical shape in three places nobody had touched: AC-2 was asserted on the wire in the scripted half but not the live half, AC-4 enumerated four of five provenance fields, and AC-9 rebuilt its own specs instead of observing the runs. The shape is easier to remove from the assertion you are looking at than from the file. When a defect class is found, sweep every assertion in the file for it in the same pass and say which ones were checked.

knowledge.title: A test that builds its own inputs cannot observe the code under test
knowledge.text: test_both_providers_are_reached_through_the_same_unchanged_spec rebuilt its AgentSpecs from the same constant the live runs used, so making the live half diverge per provider left it green: it compared a constant with itself. The fix is to record what each run actually used and assert on that. The trap survives one level down -- recording task=TASK, the module constant, rather than the local actually passed to runner.run, is the same tautology, and a mutation of the call site would still pass. Record the value that was passed, not the value it came from.

knowledge.title: Match an error class by its hierarchy, never by its name
knowledge.text: The golden eval's live retry fired only when result.error contained the string ModelError. Probed against a closed port, an unreachable gateway reports ModelProviderUnavailable, so the retry never ran for the one condition it was written for -- measured, not supposed. The condition is now derived by walking ModelError.__subclasses__() transitively, so a class added later is covered. describe_exception renders the concrete class name, which makes name-matching look sufficient and be wrong for every subclass.

knowledge.title: The live retry cannot separate a gateway hiccup from a request the gateway was right to reject
knowledge.text: The golden eval retries once on any ModelError-family failure. A malformed request the SDK built and the gateway correctly rejected surfaces as a bare ModelError, indistinguishable from a transient fault. A DETERMINISTIC bug of that shape self-reveals by failing identically on attempt 2 -- proven live in M6 round 3, where a mutation produced a real 400 from both providers and the gate stayed red. A NON-DETERMINISTIC bug of that shape would be retried away as flakiness. Nothing suggests one exists (10 clean live pairs, zero retries observed), but it is the standing price of the retry. Phase 2 should classify the boundary by HTTP status rather than by exception family: a 4xx is about the request this SDK built and must never be retried; a 429, a 5xx or a transport error is about the gateway.

knowledge.title: Genesis --reason strings pass through a shell: always single-quote them
knowledge.text: An L4 reviewer recording an M6 approval used backticks inside a double-quoted --reason, and the shell executed the backtick span as a command substitution, silently dropping a fragment of the stored text. The approval recorded correctly otherwise (3998 characters, no backticks, one clause missing). Quote every --reason and --text argument with single quotes, and keep backticks, $ and ! out of them entirely. This applies to the author as much as the reviewer.

knowledge.title: One tautological assertion survives in the golden eval, deliberately unrepaired at approval time
knowledge.text: test_the_later_phase_seams_exist_and_are_inert contains assert ApprovalRequired and InputRequired and Pending, which cannot fail because classes are always truthy. It is the last surviving instance of the coverage-not-fitness shape (KNOWLEDGE-41611bbf), reported in all three M6 rounds. Left in place at approval because the milestone gate was already green with its evidence source_hash pinned, and editing the file would have staled an approved gate to fix a low-materiality assertion over inert Phase 4/6 stubs. It belongs to the Phase 4 work that gives those stubs behaviour: a fitness assertion needs something to be wrong about, and today there is nothing.

knowledge.title: The gateway already serves the Anthropic Messages wire format, so Phase 0/1 needs no new credential
knowledge.text: Probed 2026-09-09: POST BASE_URL + /v1/messages with the EXISTING MODEL_API_KEY returns 200 in the Anthropic native shape. Accepts either x-api-key or Authorization bearer, plus anthropic-version 2023-06-01. A full tool round trip works: stop_reason tool_use with a tool_use block carrying a toolu_bdrk_ id, a tool_result block accepted back, then stop_reason end_turn and a final answer. Usage comes back Anthropic-shaped (input_tokens/output_tokens plus cache_creation and cache_read fields), not OpenAI-shaped. The /messages path without the /v1 prefix is 404. This removes the credential blocker that made a second wire format look expensive.

knowledge.title: Hold the model constant and vary only the wire format
knowledge.text: The gateway /v1/messages endpoint accepts openai.gpt-4o-mini as well as the anthropic models, translating between shapes. So the Phase 0/1 eval can send the SAME model id over two different wire formats, instead of changing model and wire format together. AC-9 varied the model and held the wire format; varying only the wire format is the mirror of it and the sharper test, because any behavioural difference can then be attributed to the adapter rather than to the model. Both directions together are what actually proves ModelClient is the only place provider shape is known.

knowledge.title: Measured: what Phase 0 store assumptions do under Phase 2 conditions
knowledge.text: Probed 2026-09-09 against the real database, all four reproduced. (A) 12 concurrent appends to ONE run: 9 commit, 3 die with UniqueViolation -- a subagent message is dropped and the caller gets a raw driver error. (B) Two PostgresEventStore sinks on one run: the second starts its in-process counter at 1 and collides immediately; 1 event stored out of 2. This is reachable by a subagent sharing a run and by ANY resumed run. (C) Six concurrent runs with a no-network model client: 0.16s wall in memory versus 4.73s with Postgres, worst single event-loop stall 1008 ms, 4.65s stalled in total. The theoretical floor is 0.15s, so persistence costs about 30x and blocks the loop for a second at a time -- which would also starve the RunHandle progress surface Phase 2 introduces. (D) One short run commits 40 transactions, each its own connect/authenticate/close.

knowledge.title: Migrations are the prerequisite for every other store fix, not a later cleanup
knowledge.text: apply_schema runs schema.sql, which is entirely CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS. On an existing database it is a no-op for anything new, so a column added to schema.sql is silently NOT created and the code then fails at insert time with an undefined-column error. Every Phase 2 store fix needs a schema change: server-side event sequence numbers, and a parent/child link between runs (the runs table has no parent_run_id, so a subagent run cannot be tied to its parent today). That makes a migration path the FIRST item in any hardening milestone rather than the last, because without it none of the others can reach an existing database.

knowledge.title: Moving most store calls off the loop is not moving them off the loop
knowledge.text: M7 round 1: FR-20 threaded the session store and the loop own emit, and left three event writes on the event loop -- RunStarted and the terminal event in api.py, and ToolCalled, which the executor called through a synchronous callback the Runner therefore could not offload. A thread-identity spy found on-loop writes on EVERY run path, not only the completed one (max turns exhausted had four). Each takes the event advisory lock, so a lock held by another process froze the whole loop: 479 ms, with an unrelated run frozen too, where the offloaded messages path stalled 14 ms under the same probe. The fix for the executor was to await whatever its emit callback returns, the rule _invoke already applied to tools. The lesson is the enumeration shape again: the offload was applied to the call sites someone looked at, not asserted as a property of every store call.

knowledge.title: Assert the property, not a stopwatch reading of its consequence
knowledge.text: M7 round 1: the NFR-8 timing tests could neither detect D1 nor stay quiet without it -- six runs passed 6 of 6 with the offload reverted, and 24 runs failed 1 in 4 with it in place, because both sat within a few milliseconds of a 50 ms bound on a Windows timer that ticks at about 15 ms. The property FR-20 names is that no store I/O runs on the event loop thread, and that is assertable exactly: a spy recording the thread each store call runs on, across every terminal path. It cannot flake because nothing in it is timed, and it failed against the unrepaired code on all four paths. Where a consequence must be measured, set the threshold far from both outcomes: a lock held for 800 ms either freezes the loop for 800 ms or not at all, so a 200 ms threshold is a detector, while 50 ms against 15 ms jitter is a coin.

knowledge.title: A guard built on a permissive parser answers a different question from its column
knowledge.text: M7: the UUID column guard used uuid.UUID(), which strips a urn:uuid: prefix that a Postgres uuid column refuses, so that form passed the guard and failed at the write with a DataError. Found by a differential -- every form the guard accepts sent to a real uuid column -- not by review, and the reviewer did not find it either. Same shape as M5 round 8, where max_turns was checked for JSON serialisability while the column was INTEGER. The guard now accepts only the canonical form, which refuses some forms the column would take; that is the safe direction. Separately, RunConfig accepted every malformed parent_run_id while its sibling fields refused theirs, and the test named for RunConfig was testing the store: a test name is a claim, and nothing checked this one.
knowledge.source: M7 round 1 D3 and the differential

knowledge.title: Repair from the recorded verdict, never from a relay, and never reuse a finding label
knowledge.text: M7 round 2 was rejected partly for a defect that was never fixed: round 1 recorded four defects and several caveats in a 3809-character reason, the relayed summary named three, and the repair worked from the summary. The author then labelled a self-found issue D4, which made the reviewer D4 disappear from every later document. Three round-1 caveats were also silently unaddressed. The fix is procedural: read the full recorded reason from project.json before repairing, build a ledger of every finding and caveat with an explicit disposition (fixed, declared, or a decision for the owner), and give self-found issues their own labels.

knowledge.title: Correction: FR-18 needed no schema change
knowledge.text: Corrects KNOWLEDGE-010d12d3 and the wording of AC-11, both of which say FR-18 needs a column that migrations must add. It needed none: event sequence numbers are computed from the stored maximum inside the insert, exactly as message sequence numbers always were. Migration 0002 serves FR-21 alone, and schema.sql is baseline 0001. AC-11 in SPEC.md still carries the wrong wording; amending the approved spec is the owner decision.

knowledge.title: Committed files are LF; this working copy is not, because the patch scripts made it CRLF
knowledge.text: Measured before the M7 round-3 commit: every file in HEAD is LF, while the working copy held 12 CRLF files and 17 LF, and the CRLF ones were exactly the files the author rewrote with Python write_text on Windows, which translates newlines to CRLF. git normalises on commit, so the diffs carry no line-ending churn (numstat identical with --ignore-cr-at-eol). That is why the round-2 prompt claimed source files were CRLF and why a reviewer found some lines LF: both described one working copy. Mutation anchors must normalise newlines, and nothing should claim the repository itself is mixed. This also corrects the line-ending wording in DECISION-01de1095, whose conclusion to hash newline-normalised text still stands.

knowledge.title: Correction: working-copy line endings depend on what last wrote each file
knowledge.text: Corrects KNOWLEDGE-0bc27060, which attributed every CRLF file in the working copy to the author Python patch scripts. Measured after M7 round 3: core.autocrlf is true in the system gitconfig and there is no .gitattributes, so git checks files out as CRLF and commits LF. Files the Write tool created and git never re-checked out stay LF (agentsdk/__init__.py, agentsdk/tools.py, tests/test_agent_loop.py); files written by a git checkout or by Python write_text on Windows are CRLF; and a file a tool has just rewritten can be in either state until git normalises it on commit. That is why a reviewer saw LF lines where the round-2 prompt said CRLF: both described real moments. HEAD is LF throughout. Mutation anchors must tolerate either ending.

knowledge.title: mcp 2.x renamed the server class and moved every field to snake_case
knowledge.text: Measured with mcp 2.2.0, the version pip resolves today: from mcp.server.fastmcp import FastMCP fails with ModuleNotFoundError, because FastMCP was renamed MCPServer (from mcp.server.mcpserver import MCPServer), constructed as MCPServer(name) with the same @app.tool() decorator and app.run() defaulting to stdio. The client imports are unchanged (from mcp import ClientSession, StdioServerParameters; from mcp.client.stdio import stdio_client), but result and listing fields are snake_case: Tool.input_schema not inputSchema, CallToolResult.is_error not isError. A stdio round trip through list_tools and call_tool returned TextContent. Most published MCP examples are 1.x and fail against this version, the first by crashing the server so the client reports only Connection closed.

knowledge.title: PostgresTrace.reconstruct returns the manifest as a bare positional row
knowledge.text: Found by running scripts/04 live during M8. reconstruct returns run as a dict and messages and events as lists of dicts, but manifest as the raw fetchone() tuple of eight columns in SELECT order: sdk_version, agent_spec_hash, instructions_hash, model_id, model_version, model_adapter_version, tool_spec_hashes, policy_version. A caller treating it like the rest of the trace fails; sorted() over it raised TypeError comparing the tool_spec_hashes list with a string. The M8 gate could not see this, because it runs examples offline and only a live run with a database reaches that code. M8 adds no SDK capability, so the example prints the row as it comes; returning a dict is a candidate change for the next SDK milestone.

knowledge.title: A run whose model comes from the client default records no model id
knowledge.text: Seen running scripts/04 live in M8. The agent named no preferred_model and one client was registered, so the Runner resolved that client with model_id None; the client sent its own default model, but the runs row stored model_id NULL and the manifest recorded model_id unspecified and model_version unregistered. The run completed against a real model and nothing persisted says which one. FR-11 exists to answer what configuration produced a run, and this path cannot. The persisting examples now name the model on the agent. Candidate SDK change: resolve the client default model id into the run row and manifest when no model is named.

knowledge.title: Gateway usage accounting: cached and reasoning tokens are subsets
knowledge.text: Measured 2026-09-12 through the LiteLLM gateway. gpt-4o-mini with a repeated 2620 token prompt reported prompt_tokens 2620 and prompt_tokens_details.cached_tokens 2560, so cached tokens are inside prompt_tokens. Claude Haiku with reasoning_effort low reported completion_tokens 45 with completion_tokens_details.reasoning_tokens 25 and text_tokens 20, so reasoning tokens are inside completion_tokens. Bedrock responses also carry top level cache_read_input_tokens and cache_creation_input_tokens plus prompt_tokens_details.cache_write_tokens. GET /model/info returns 403, so no prices come from the gateway. At finish_reason length, gpt-4o-mini returned a tool call with undecodable arguments and Claude Haiku returned one whose arguments decoded.

knowledge.title: Reasoning effort on Claude over the gateway
knowledge.text: Measured 2026-09-12. Claude Haiku with reasoning_effort low and max_tokens 1024 returns HTTP 400 because max_tokens must be greater than thinking.budget_tokens; with no max_tokens it succeeds, and responses then carry reasoning_content and thinking_blocks. A two turn tool loop that sent back only content and tool_calls, without thinking blocks, returned HTTP 200 with 0 reasoning tokens on turn 2. gpt-4o-mini accepted reasoning_effort low without error.

knowledge.title: Host limits for filesystem and HTTP confinement tests
knowledge.text: Measured 2026-09-12 on this Windows host. os.symlink fails with WinError 1314 for files and directories without Developer Mode, while _winapi.CreateJunction, os.link hard links and alternate data streams all succeed, and a hard link reports st_nlink 2. httpx 0.28.1 defaults to trust_env True, which honours environment proxy variables such as HTTP_PROXY; netrc credentials are used only through an explicit NetRCAuth.

knowledge.title: repr of Persistence exposes the database password
knowledge.text: Persistence is a frozen dataclass whose first field is the raw DSN string, so repr(Persistence) and str(Persistence) print the database URL with its password. Verified 2026-09-12 with a fake DSN: the fake password appears in both, while repr(PostgresRunStore) does not show it. Reported by the M9 round 1 reviewer as an M8 finding recorded nowhere. It is contrary to NFR-4, which Secret exists to enforce: a log line, an exception message or a debugger that renders the Persistence object reveals the credential. Not an M9 defect. A one-field repr=False change closes it; open until the owner schedules the fix.
knowledge.source: M9 round 1 L4 review, verified by the implementing session

knowledge.title: Cancelling a run loses its billed cost and leaves the row running
knowledge.text: Reproduced by the M9 round 2 L4 reviewer. After one billed call, asyncio.CancelledError propagates through Runner.run under the project rule that cancellation is control flow, so no RunResult is returned and finish_run is never called: a persisted run stays status running with NULL usage and cost, and the cost already billed is reported nowhere. Before M9 there was no cost to lose. A candidate for Phase 6, which owns pause, resume and cancel.

knowledge.title: A recorder that omits records_accounting silently stores no usage or cost
knowledge.text: Since M9 round 2 the Runner passes usage and cost to a run recorder only when it declares records_accounting = True. A custom recorder with the new finish_run signature that forgets the flag receives usage None and cost_usd None while RunResult reports the real cost, with no error. Round 1 inferred support from the signature, and a wrapped pre-M9 recorder failed runs loudly; the declaration trades that loud failure for this silent one. PostgresRunStore declares the flag, so only custom recorders are affected.

knowledge.title: A rate limit with a slow error body can take about 16.5 seconds to fail
knowledge.text: M9 round 2 bounds each error body read to error_body_timeout, default 5 seconds per attempt. Under default settings a rate limited call whose body trickles takes about 16.5 seconds to fail: three attempts at 5 seconds plus backoff of 0.5 and 1 second, where before M9 it failed almost at once. No NFR constrains error path latency; a caller that cares can lower error_body_timeout on the client. Measured by the M9 round 2 L4 reviewer.

knowledge.title: Two thirds of stored runs are test debris left at status running
knowledge.text: Measured 2026-09-12: 20455 of 30447 runs are status running, 20417 of them in tenant t-test, started 2026-09-06 to 2026-09-12; no real or example tenant is affected. 756 running rows carry a RunCompleted (746) or RunFailed (20) event. 722 of those are t-test rows with agent_spec_id spec-1, written by store level tests in tests/test_persistence.py that start a run and emit events directly with no finish_run and no cleanup; the suite added 24 more that day. The other 34 are Runner test runs (t-unreg, t-e2e, t-fail, t-store and others), all started 2026-09-06 to 2026-09-08 and none since, and every t-unreg run from 2026-09-09 on completed, so no current code path leaves a Runner run unfinished. A which-runs-are-live query against this database returns mostly test debris. Found by the M9 round 2 L4 reviewer; characterised by the implementing session. Worth cleaning before Phase 2 builds orchestration on run status.
knowledge.source: M9 round 2 L4 review and implementing session query, 2026-09-12

knowledge.title: The repr of Persistence no longer shows the database password
knowledge.text: Closes the exposure recorded in KNOWLEDGE-cb2f13f5, with owner approval on 2026-09-12, in the commit titled Hide the database password from repr(Persistence). Persistence.dsn is field(repr=False). A test in tests/test_model_client.py renders every object a Persistence hands out six ways (repr, str, an f-string, percent-r, pprint, inside an exception) and was red before the fix. Extraction by persistence.dsn, vars or dataclasses.asdict still returns the DSN by design, because the stores need it.

knowledge.title: Stuck test runs purged, and the store tests now remove what they write
knowledge.text: Follows KNOWLEDGE-322ef7f4. On 2026-09-12, with owner approval and after a rolled back dry run of the same statements, one transaction deleted the 20487 runs at status running in tenants t and t-*, with 6499 run_events, 21266 messages and 19515 execution_manifests rows. After: 10020 runs, none running, 22 runs without a manifest (was 994, so 972 of that long standing baseline were these stuck test runs), and no event, message or manifest row without its run. tests/test_persistence.py now removes every run each test writes under tenant t or t-* and fails at module teardown if any remain; one run of the file left 47 runs before the fixture and none after. Future reviews should expect 22 manifest-less runs, not 994.

knowledge.title: Developer Mode is on: this host can now create symlinks for M10
knowledge.text: Updates KNOWLEDGE-083e000b. On 2026-09-12, with owner approval, Windows Developer Mode was turned on (HKLM AppModelUnlock AllowDevelopmentWithoutDevLicense = 1, set through an elevation prompt the owner accepted). Unprivileged os.symlink then created a file symlink and a directory symlink, and the file symlink resolved to and read its target. The M10 precondition of decision D7 is met: AC-28 symlink escape cases can run and fail rather than skip.

knowledge.title: Correction: KNOWLEDGE-c783cf3f was recorded before its verification ran
knowledge.text: KNOWLEDGE-c783cf3f states that unprivileged symlink creation was verified after Developer Mode was turned on. When it was written, that was not yet true: a line continuation after a heredoc broke the verification script, which crashed on its first line with NameError, and the shell chain recorded the knowledge anyway instead of stopping. A standalone verification then ran on 2026-09-12 and confirmed the claim: a file symlink and a directory symlink were created without elevation, the file symlink is a symlink, resolves to its target and reads its content. The facts in KNOWLEDGE-c783cf3f hold; the order in which it was recorded did not follow the rule that gates are computed, not narrated.

knowledge.title: httpx drops a default or empty port when parsing, so allowlist ports must be refused by spelling
knowledge.text: Measured 2026-09-13 with httpx 0.28.1. httpx.URL reports port None for http://allowed.test:80/ and for http://allowed.test:/, and likewise for [::1]:80, so a check on the parsed port accepted allowlist entries that name a port. M10 fetch_tool now refuses any colon outside IPv6 brackets in an entry. httpx also refuses to parse numeric hosts with leading-zero octets such as 0177.0.0.1 and 127.000.000.001 (InvalidURL), while 127.1, 2130706433, 0x7f000001 and 0x7f.0.0.1 parse as names, so a numeric host spelling must be interpreted by the tool and never passed to DNS.

knowledge.title: The venv python.exe is a launcher, so a subprocess timeout kills only the launcher
knowledge.text: Measured 2026-09-13 on this host. The venv python.exe starts a child python3.11.exe from the Store install. subprocess.run with a timeout killed only the launcher and then waited on the pipes the real interpreter still held, so an M10 mutant with a 900 second limit ran about 40 minutes. Stopping that harness mid-mutant skipped its restore and left the mutation in an untracked file with no git copy; it was found by searching for mutation markers and restored. Harnesses on this host use Popen with taskkill /T /F on timeout, and any interrupted mutation run is followed by a search for mutation markers.

knowledge.title: Building an httpx client costs about 0.4 seconds here, so check before connecting
knowledge.text: Measured 2026-09-13. A refused fetch that built an httpx.AsyncClient with default verification before checking the URL took 0.41 s, and the M10 corpus of about 5000 refused address answers ran for over half an hour. httpx.create_ssl_context with trust_env False took 0.28 s once and is cached; fetch_tool now builds its client only after a hop passes every check, and the corpus runs in about a second.

knowledge.title: An open handle without delete sharing pins a Windows directory and its parent
knowledge.text: Measured 2026-09-13 on NTFS. CreateFileW with FILE_FLAG_BACKUP_SEMANTICS and share mode read and write, without delete, opens a directory. While that handle is open, renaming the directory fails with winerror 32 and renaming its parent with winerror 5, and an open file handle also blocks renaming its parent. GetFinalPathNameByHandleW on such a handle returns the path after every symlink and junction, and GetFileInformationByHandleEx with FileFullDirectoryInfo enumerates the directory through the handle. The M10 file tools rest on these facts. Retargeting an existing junction in place was not measured.

knowledge.title: File tools and every store call share one default thread pool, which a burst of file tools starves
knowledge.text: M10 independent review round 1, measured by the reviewer on this host with 20 default workers: store to_thread latency peaked at 125 ms with 19 concurrent greps, 139 s with 20 and 299 s with 28. Mechanism confirmed by the implementing session on 2026-09-13: agentsdk calls asyncio.to_thread in builtin_tools, api, loop and postgres (17 call sites) and defines no executor of its own, so every call shares the loop default pool, sized min(32, cpu_count + 4). A worker thread cannot be interrupted after the executor timeout, so a saturated pool stalls persistence for every run, including runs that call no file tool. NFR-8 still holds because it measures event loop stall, not store latency.
knowledge.source: M10 L4 review round 1 (control 158234c3), mechanism confirmed 2026-09-13

knowledge.title: A synchronous search backend iterable blocks the event loop
knowledge.text: M10 independent review caveat 3, confirmed by reading web_search_tool on 2026-09-13: the tool awaits backend.search and then iterates what it returned on the event loop, so a synchronous generator that keeps yielding malformed items, or blocks between items, holds the loop past the executor timeout. It is caller code and not reachable by a model. Recorded, not fixed in M10.

knowledge.title: Fetch TLS re-verification across redirects rests on redirect bodies never being read
knowledge.text: M10 independent review caveat 6. fetch_tool rewrites each request to the checked address, and the connection pool keys connections by scheme, address and port. The reviewer found that a redirect to a second allowlisted host gets a freshly verified connection today only because the redirect response is closed without its body being read. A change that drains redirect bodies, or two allowlisted hosts on one address, could serve the second host over a connection verified for the first. Recorded, not fixed in M10; a change there needs a test with two hosts on one address.

knowledge.title: Glob and grep return no matches in a folder of more than 100000 entries
knowledge.text: M10 independent review round 2, caveat 4, measured by the reviewer: a flat folder above the 100000-entry walk limit lists 100168 entries, so glob and grep return no matches with the search stopped early note even for a file whose literal name exists. Bounded and labelled, so the model is told the search was incomplete. Recorded, not fixed in M10.

knowledge.title: Glob keeps opening matches after it has found max_results
knowledge.text: M10 independent review round 2, caveat 5, measured by the reviewer: with 30000 matching files glob took 6.7 s and ended with results cut at 1000, because it opens every match to check where it resolves until the walk ends instead of stopping once it holds more than max_results. Bounded by the walk budget. Recorded, not fixed in M10.

knowledge.title: A check must guard the value that is used: read an untrusted field once
knowledge.text: M10 review round 3 rejected the executor (control 4640a946), confirmed first-hand 2026-09-13. Step 8 checked type(returned.is_error) is bool on one read and built the returned ToolResult from a second read, so a ToolResult subclass built past its constructor answered True and then NOT-A-BOOL or 5 MB of text; the run completed, persisted it, and passed the 40-character output cap through a field the cap does not measure. Provenance fields were never type-checked, so a plain-string origin completed in memory and raised on origin.value in the Postgres serialiser and the context assembler. Rule for any value caller code shapes: read each field exactly once into a local, check that local for type and size, and build only from the checked locals. A test for it needs a value that changes between reads; fixed values set with object.__setattr__ cannot expose a second read.

knowledge.title: Fetch refuses a final URL over 8192 characters, after the request is sent
knowledge.text: M10 independent review round 5, caveat 1, measured by the reviewer. A fetched final URL of 8192 characters completes; 8193, 9000 and 50000 through redirects become a tool error naming the source bound, with the declared external labels kept (D12) and ToolCalled is_error true, identical on memory and Postgres. A model URL of 2048 code points, inside the input schema limit, can percent-encode past 8192 and is refused only after its request was sent. It fails closed. Mutant R5-D (the bound written as >= instead of >) survived the full suite: no test pins the exact 8192 to 8193 boundary. Recorded, not fixed in M10.

knowledge.title: A str subclass source is refused where it completed before M10
knowledge.text: M10 independent review round 5, caveat 2, reproduced first-hand 2026-09-13 through the public Runner on memory and Postgres. A ContentProvenance whose source_uri_or_hash is a str subclass, from an after_tool hook or a custom tool ToolOutput, completed before M10; step 8 now returns a tool error saying the source is not text of at most 8192 characters. This is ordinary caller code, not forgery under DECISION-2bad84bb: a narrow regression that fails closed. Carry to the next milestone: copy the source into an exact str as _text does for content, and add a test that pins the 8192 to 8193 boundary.
knowledge.source: M10 L4 review round 5 (control ff8cd80c), reproduced 2026-09-13

knowledge.title: Forged enum labels pass ResultProvenance and reach the error path unchecked
knowledge.text: M10 independent review round 5, caveat 3, outside the threat model under DECISION-2bad84bb. Origin(forged) returns a str.__new__ forged instance unchanged, so ResultProvenance accepts a forged label and _failed carries it without _checked_provenance. Mutant R5-C (dropping the exact frozenset check on taint flags) survived the full suite because ContentProvenance already coerces a set to a frozenset, so only forgery reaches that check: defence in depth, not a gate gap over reachable code. Recorded, not fixed.

knowledge.title: Facts the Phase 2 increment 1 spec reviews measured in the code
knowledge.text: Read-only reviews on 2026-09-14. ToolSpec.read_only defaults to True. InMemoryEventSink.emit numbers events with len() and then appends, and 8 threads produced duplicate sequence_no values. The Postgres event sink appends to its local list after the insert commits, so events() can be out of sequence_no order. runs.status has an unnamed column CHECK; run_events.event_type has none. Cancelling an asyncio.to_thread store write does not stop a thread already running and drops one still queued. Every store call and every file tool share the default executor. psycopg reads BYTEA as text by default. On this host time.monotonic has 15.625 ms resolution and time.perf_counter 100 ns. The released OpenTelemetry semantic conventions name the cache attribute gen_ai.usage.cache_creation.input_tokens.

knowledge.title: M11 pre-flight: baseline suite, carry-over reproductions and runs left behind
knowledge.text: Measured 2026-09-14 at commit 7abfe47, before any M11 change. The full suite passed 821 tests in 132.8 s on Python 3.11.9. A probe on the unchanged code reproduced the FR-47 carry-overs: over a folder holding a file and a subfolder named with a lone surrogate, list_directory, glob and grep each returned a ToolExecutionError naming UnicodeEncodeError at the executor storability check; a ToolOutput whose source is a str subclass was refused as not text of at most 8192 characters; sources of 8192 characters passed and 8193 were refused. After that full run, 13 runs written in the previous 20 minutes remained in the store, all from tests/test_golden_eval.py: t-ac1 to t-ac4, t-nfr3, t-nfr4 and t-seams one each, t-principal four and t-live two. The M11 tests written first then failed 88 and passed 6 against the unchanged code; the 6 were the existing source bound checks on both stores.
knowledge.source: M11 pre-flight probe and red run, 2026-09-14

knowledge.title: M11 round 1 review: R1 to R3 repaired, R1 judged blocking by the owner
knowledge.text: Round 1 (Claude Fable 5.1, 2026-09-14, control 0e6eca38) approved M11 with caveats R1 to R5. The owner reran the reviewer probes and judged R1 blocking, because FR-44 states that a BaseException escaping a call cancels and awaits its siblings, and CancelledError is one. R1: asyncio.wait with FIRST_EXCEPTION does not wake for a task that ends cancelled, so a call ending in CancelledError left its siblings running to their own end; a sibling with no timeout held the run open without bound and kept running after the run failed. R2: a second cancel landing in the finally await left the cancelled siblings unawaited, 4 tasks pending after the run ended. R3: glob with ** or **/* counted a withheld folder twice, 3 where there are 2. Repairs: the batch wait uses FIRST_COMPLETED and treats a cancelled task as an escape; a new cancel-and-wait absorbs further cancellation until every sibling has finished, then re-raises the original; glob counts an unstorable entry once per directory and name. Tests written first failed against the round 1 code: TimeoutError at a 5 s bound for R1, cleaned [] for R2, 3 withheld for R3. R4 (the AC-44 check keyed on run ids, the golden-eval cleanup by t- tenant and start time) and R5 (KeyboardInterrupt and SystemExit left to asyncio.run) are unchanged and declared. The round 1 approval covered source hash 76d9c077 only; a round 2 review on a different model is required before M11 is marked done.
knowledge.source: M11 review round 1 control 0e6eca38 and the owner recheck, 2026-09-14

knowledge.title: Assumption review 2026-09-14: three resolved, two still open
knowledge.text: Genesis records assumptions without a command to change their status, so this note records their state. Resolved: ASSUMPTION-bba5b3f6 (the Postgres superuser password unknown to the harness) is superseded by ASSUMPTION-6c8f0f59, whose own text says so. ASSUMPTION-6c8f0f59 (the development database exists and is reachable) is verified: every database-backed gate since M5 has run against it, and SPEC.md already lists it as resolved. ASSUMPTION-75110765 (two M3 limitations) was closed in M9 under FR-33 and AC-26: _error_text in providers/openai_compatible.py treats any failure to read an error body as unreadable, so a 429 is ModelRateLimited and retried whatever its body, and _scrub removes the credential from 2xx bodies as well as error bodies, citing this assumption by id. Rerun 2026-09-14: the AC-26 tests in tests/test_honest_results.py, 54 passed. Still open: ASSUMPTION-53240ce4 (the Docker daemon is not running; not needed while the native Postgres service works) and ASSUMPTION-b7463ca2 (a billed call with no usage reported is not counted; to be closed with the native Anthropic adapter per DECISION-0e3ed41b).
knowledge.source: assumption review 2026-09-14, code read and AC-26 rerun

knowledge.title: M12 pre-flight: baseline, the sink race and a cancelled run left running
knowledge.text: Measured 2026-09-14 at commit 1662ede, before any M12 change. The full suite passed 925 tests in 122 s. InMemoryEventSink numbers an event by reading its length and then appending: at the default thread switch interval, 8 threads emitting 500 events each for 20 trials produced no duplicate sequence_no, but with sys.setswitchinterval(1e-6), 8 threads emitting 300 events each produced between 584 and 654 duplicates in each of 10 trials, so a test of FR-52 must shorten the switch interval to detect the race. KNOWLEDGE-b3c2b462 reproduced on Postgres: a persisted run whose model client waited inside send was cancelled through the task awaiting Runner.run; Runner.run raised CancelledError, and the stored row stayed status running with NULL usage, NULL cost and no completed_at, with RunStarted its only event. The live database is at migration 0004, and runs.status carries one check constraint, named runs_status_check, admitting running, completed, failed and max_turns_exceeded. Owner decision DECISION-29e21dd0 makes a tool that ignores cancellation a declared limitation.

knowledge.title: KNOWLEDGE-b3c2b462 closed by M12: a cancelled run is recorded cancelled
knowledge.text: Closed 2026-09-15 by M12 (FR-50), approved in L4 review round 1 by Claude Fable 5.1. The M12 pre-flight reproduced it on Postgres (KNOWLEDGE-93fa7f44): a run cancelled through the task awaiting Runner.run stayed status running with NULL usage and cost. Cancellation now ends the run with status cancelled and RunCancelled as its last event; runs.status is cancelled with usage recorded, the cost is NULL when a model call was in flight (P2-D7), and CancelledError still reaches the caller. tests/test_run_handles.py covers cancellation at every point on both stores, and the reviewer fuzzed 1100 runs with no run left running.
knowledge.source: M12 FR-50 and L4 review round 1, 2026-09-15

knowledge.title: M12 round 1 review: approved with caveats C1 to C4
knowledge.text: Claude Fable 5.1 approved M12 on 2026-09-15 at source c4ea020a after re-deriving FR-48 to FR-52 and probing absorbed cancellation, cancellation from hooks and tools, pairing under ToolCalled lock contention, 300 iterators, and a randomised fuzz of 1000 in-memory and 100 Postgres runs with 0 violations. The owner rechecked the reviewer and reproduced C1. C1: RunHandle.cancel called from a thread other than the run loop thread calls Task.cancel directly, so it takes effect only when the loop next wakes, and under asyncio debug mode Task.cancel raises RuntimeError and the run is stuck. Owner decision: fixed as a follow-up after the M12 commit by scheduling the cancel with call_soon_threadsafe, with no new review round. C2: migration 0005 also drops a multi-column CHECK mentioning status without restoring it, which schema.sql cannot produce. C3: a call cancelled while waiting for the ToolCalled lock at step 9 is recorded ToolCancelled, consistent with FR-44. C4: a BaseException other than CancelledError from a tool still leaves no terminal event, as before M12 and outside NFR-17. The reviewer regression gate took 398 s against 152 s in the author run, cause unknown, both passing.
knowledge.source: M12 L4 review round 1 control and owner recheck, 2026-09-15

knowledge.title: M12 review caveat C1 fixed: cancel() from another thread is handed to the run loop
knowledge.text: Owner-approved follow-up to the M12 round 1 review (KNOWLEDGE-a23d69bd), fixed on 2026-09-15 with no new review round. RunControl.request, called off the run event loop thread, now hands the cancel to that loop with call_soon_threadsafe, and the scheduled callback cancels the task only if the run has not ended or begun its terminal write; Runner.start records the loop, and RunHandle.cancel says it may be called from any thread. Written first, test_cancel_called_from_another_thread_takes_effect_promptly failed against the unchanged handle on both stores: in normal mode the run did not end within 5 s, and in asyncio debug mode cancel() raised RuntimeError on the calling thread. Its first version ran in the test event loop and hung the session at teardown for more than 300 s in debug mode, because a task whose awaited future was cancelled from another thread under debug mode can never be woken; that session was killed and left no runs behind, and the test now runs its scenario on its own event loop in a daemon thread joined with a bound. After the fix: test_run_handles and test_concurrency 168 passed, full suite 989 passed in 189 s.

knowledge.title: M13 pre-flight: baseline, BYTEA reads, and what the artifact store touches
knowledge.text: Measured 2026-09-15 at commit e366ded, before any M13 change. The full suite passed 989 tests in 132 s. psycopg 3.3.5 against PostgreSQL 16.13 returns a BYTEA value as Python bytes from both a text and a binary cursor: the risk that reads carry hex describes the text wire format, not the Python type. A 10485760-byte round trip took 142 ms through a text cursor and 99 ms through a binary one, both equal to the input, with a Python peak of 21 MB, so the store reads content through a binary cursor. The executor step 8 provenance check, _checked_provenance with _is_member and _MAX_SOURCE_CHARS, is referenced only inside agentsdk/executor.py, so FR-53 can move it to primitives without touching a test. The README and scripts/README.md list examples in tables, and no test checked that listing before M13.

knowledge.title: Transient gateway failure in the live golden eval during M13
knowledge.text: M13 full suite on the uncommitted M13 tree, 2026-09-15: 1 failed, 1090 passed in 227.45 s. The failure was tests/test_golden_eval.py::test_the_same_eval_passes_against_a_live_provider[openai.gpt-4o-mini]: the live run completed but needed 2 attempts, because its first model call failed at the gateway with ModelProviderUnavailable (upstream connect error or disconnect/reset before headers, reset reason connection termination), and the test requires exactly one attempt. Rerun alone with no other test process: 2 passed in 21.10 s. First recorded occurrence, not reproduced; treated as a transient gateway failure, not an M13 defect. If it recurs, decide whether the live eval should tolerate a recorded retry.

knowledge.title: M13 independent review round 1
knowledge.text: Independent review round 1 of M13-artifacts: Claude Sonnet 5 approved at 2026-09-15T12:47:22Z and raised no new findings; its gate run passed 121 and 1110 on source hash 883c13df. The owner checked the reviewer: code unchanged, no worktrees or stashes, every database table back to its starting count, no leftover processes. The reviewer skipped the top item of the brief, tenant and project scope, so the owner verified it on both stores: every statement on artifacts filters by tenant and project, reads and delete also by expiry, and the insert checks the source run scope in the same statement; all 33 lookups per store (a missing id, another project, another tenant, another project through for_scope, an expired artifact, four non-canonical id forms, an integer, None) raised ArtifactNotFound with a message naming only the id as given; delete and expire from another scope removed nothing; only a source run of the store scope was accepted. Reviewer probes rerun by the owner: a cancel while the insert fails leaves 0 rows; asyncio.timeout around a held put raises TimeoutError and leaves 0 rows; deleting a run that an artifact names is refused by the foreign key; a changed content_hash raises ArtifactIntegrityError. Caveats, not findings: a changed size is reported as stored (declared); a non-UTC expires_at reads back on Postgres in the database zone (+05:30) and in memory in the offset given, the same instant (cosmetic). Not probed by the reviewer and covered only by the author tests: a bytes subclass as content, the injected clock at exactly the expiry boundary, a cancel before the worker thread starts or during the clean-up of a cancelled put, and the provenance move into primitives (mutants A3, A9, E1 and the unchanged M10 provenance tests).

knowledge.title: M14 pre-flight: baseline, telemetry packages, semantic conventions and two spec gaps
knowledge.text: Baseline at 22d71c6 with no other python or node process: 1110 passed in 136.07 s. Installed opentelemetry-sdk and opentelemetry-exporter-otlp-proto-http 1.44.0 (opentelemetry-api 1.44.0 was already present as a dependency of mcp); the resolver added opentelemetry-proto and opentelemetry-exporter-otlp-proto-common 1.44.0, opentelemetry-semantic-conventions 0.65b0, protobuf 7.36.1, googleapis-common-protos 1.75.3, requests 2.34.2, urllib3 2.7.0 and charset-normalizer 3.5.1, upgrading nothing, and pip check is clean. The three pins are in requirements.txt below the test line, in scripts/requirements.txt and in a new otel extra; tests/test_distribution.py checks only the examples extra, so the new extra needs no test edit. Semantic conventions: the 0.65b0 package carries schema versions up to 1.43.0, including 1.40.0, and all twelve attribute names FR-59 lists and the operation values invoke_agent, chat and execute_tool are present in it (checked in the package, not against the v1.40.0 registry). Code facts for FR-57: ModelRequest has no model field; the model travels in model_settings under model and is priced from there (cost_of in api.py); the provider slot wait and send are adjacent in loop.py; a tool call enters its slots in ToolExecutor.run_prepared immediately before step 6; the three terminal emits are in Runner._drive (failed), Runner._cancelled and Runner._run; RunEvent already carries a timestamp; no test compares a whole event payload. Two gaps were found and decided by the owner in the M14 parent and provider decision. The Docker daemon is now running (29.6.2), so ASSUMPTION-53240ce4 no longer holds.

knowledge.title: M14 round 1 review: approved with caveats C1 to C9
knowledge.text: Opus 5 in a fresh session approved M14-timings-and-telemetry round 1 with nine caveats and no blocker, reporting every Attack item as probed, and reran both gates on a clean tree (unit 78, regression 1188, source hash 6ce35a78). The owner reran eight of its saved probe scripts and matched every result (the C8 loop stall measured 30 ms against the reviewer 60 ms), queried Jaeger for the live trace (5 spans under invoke_agent calendar), and found no repo file, database row, process or container left behind. Caveats: C1 export of a RunHandle from another thread event loop can hang that loop events iterator and flush when the loop ends or runs in debug mode, because handle.py _wake empties its waiter list and then wakes each waiter, so one raising strands the rest; C2 a before_model hook naming the model as a StrEnum member or a str subclass is recorded as the run model while the call is priced as the named one, against AC-45; C3 a tool name the model invents is exported as gen_ai.tool.name; C4 exceeding MAX_OPEN_RUNS exports empty spans; C5 a dropped RunStarted also loses one child span; C6 exporting a run twice duplicates or garbles its span tree; C7 a SystemExit raised in a span processor stops the worker without counting an error; C8 a CPU-heavy span processor stalls the event loop; C9 export(handle) with no running loop raises RuntimeError to the caller.

knowledge.title: M14 round 2 review: approved with caveats R1 and R2 and five test gaps
knowledge.text: Fable 5.1 in a fresh session approved M14-timings-and-telemetry round 2 (the C1 and C2 fixes of DECISION-95a84cb0) at source hash f131773d, with caveats R1 and R2 and five test gaps, and reported every attack item and bullet as probed. The owner reran items 1 to 4 on the intact tree: the C2 fix consistent in 26 of 28 probe cases on both stores, as the reviewer found (a StrEnum member, str subclasses overriding __str__, __eq__, __len__ and __getitem__, and unstorable, whitespace, non-text and empty names), with event, result, runs row and wire payload agreeing; the C1 fix through the exporter 20 of 20; and a foreign-loop follow leaving results, events and stored rows identical on both stores 4 of 4. Nothing was left behind. During the review the reviewer stalled once and was resumed, reported completed while its own mutation run was still mutating a repo file (the owner waited for that process to exit and checked file hashes before resuming it), needed three gate runs (a gateway connection reset in a live test, then a unit gate made stale by .pytest_cache), and ran example 13 live once, adding a Jaeger trace and no database rows. R1: an events() iterator on another thread event loop can receive every event and never end, because handle.py _stream checks _ended and then appends its waiter without checking again; the owner saw it hang in 7 and 6 of 10 trials on Postgres with a debug-mode loop and 3 in 400 in memory; no run was affected, FR-48 keeps readers on the run loop, and the exporter follows on that loop. The round 2 _wake docstring and author issue B4 overstate that iterators on other loops are safe, and the test pinning it runs only in memory, where the timing hides the race. R2: a before_model hook that replaces model_settings with a MappingProxyType is recorded and priced as the run model while the client sends the model it names; model_settings is typed dict, and round 1 behaved the same. Test gaps where the code is correct: a str subclass overriding __str__ or __len__; the done check in _resolve; flush with several followed handles; and a stopped but unclosed run loop treated as running, which went undetected except as a 599 s suite instead of about 170 s.

knowledge.title: M15 pre-flight (FR-63): the Claude Agent SDK runs against the gateway
knowledge.text: Recorded before any live comparison (AC-49). Baseline at 6cacf5e with no other python or node process: 1199 passed in 166.64 s. Gateway, probed directly over the Anthropic Messages endpoint at BASE_URL /v1/messages with the existing credential: HTTP 200 with the x-api-key header, HTTP 200 with an Authorization Bearer header, and HTTP 200 with the anthropic-beta header claude-code-20250219 that the Claude Code CLI sends, each answering with model bedrock.anthropic.claude-haiku-4-5 and stop_reason end_turn; the plain model id claude-haiku-4-5 is refused with HTTP 400 and Invalid model name, so the gateway id is required. Usage comes back as input_tokens, output_tokens, cache_read_input_tokens and cache_creation_input_tokens, which is what FR-62 normalises for the Claude arm. Python side: claude-agent-sdk 0.2.152 installed into the repository venv, adding only itself and sniffio, upgrading nothing, and pip check is clean; ClaudeAgentOptions carries tools, allowed_tools, permission_mode (dontAsk is a valid value), setting_sources, cwd, env, model, max_turns and cli_path, so FR-61 configuration maps one to one. The Claude Code CLI, which the Python SDK spawns, was absent from the machine (not on PATH, nothing in the npm global prefix, nothing under the home directory): the owner chose a local pinned install under evals/adr12 (see the M15 CLI decision), version 2.1.267, and the package ships bin/claude.exe, which avoids the npm cmd shim the SDK refuses on Windows. Live Claude arm through that CLI, with tools Read, Glob and Grep, permission_mode dontAsk, setting_sources empty, a fixture folder outside the repository as cwd, and ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL, ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN, ANTHROPIC_MODEL, ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_HAIKU_MODEL and CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_NONESSENTIAL_TRAFFIC set as FR-61 requires: it answered the one-file question correctly (fox) in 2 turns, is_error false, its own cost estimate 0.00607, wall time 5.1 s, and reported the usage fields above. The CLI also printed a warning that claude.ai connectors are disabled because an auth source is set, which is the intended configuration. Outcome: FR-63 is satisfied and M15 does not stop.

knowledge.title: M15 live ADR-12 comparison: what it measured
knowledge.text: The live report is evals/adr12/reports/adr12-comparison-2026-09-16.json and .md, dated 2026-09-16T09:13:04Z: 12 tasks by 2 arms by 3 repetitions, 72 rows, 71 checkers passed, no credential and no gateway host in either file. Model bedrock.anthropic.claude-haiku-4-5 through the same gateway for both arms; versions agentsdk 0.1.0.dev0 (OpenAI-compatible chat completions) and claude-agent-sdk 0.2.152 with Claude Code CLI 2.1.267 (Anthropic Messages through the CLI). Both arms costed from one price list, input 0.000001 and output 0.000005 per token, which is the published Haiku 4.5 rate, so the Claude arm own estimate and the computed cost agree. Results: this SDK 35 of 36 checkers passed, 69687 prompt and 3473 completion tokens, cost 0.0871, median 2 turns, median wall 3723 ms; the Claude Agent SDK 36 of 36, 303691 prompt and 10796 completion tokens, cost 0.3577, median 3 turns, median wall 6140 ms. By kind both arms passed every single-step, long and decline run; the only failure was one multi-step run. That failure is a transient gateway outage, not an SDK defect: ModelProviderUnavailable on key-holding-the-region repetition 2, which the same task passed on both arms in the other two repetitions. Two findings for the second increment and for Phase 5A. First, the Claude arm spends about 4.4 times the prompt tokens and about 4.1 times the cost for the same tasks and the same model, at about 1.6 times the median wall time, which is the price of its system prompt and tool preamble; this SDK sends only what the task needs. Second, the failed run took 2555071 ms, about 42.6 minutes, with one turn recorded: the HTTP client timeout of 60 seconds is a per read timeout rather than a deadline for the whole call, and the retry policy is 3 attempts, so a response that trickles can stall a run for tens of minutes. Nothing bounds one model call end to end today; the comparison harness applies no deadline of its own either. An earlier live run of the same comparison read every correct decline as a failure, because the checker wanted cannot or unable or no tool while both arms answered that they do not have the ability to delete files; the checker was widened to the spellings the arms use and the whole comparison was rerun, so this report reflects one checker version.

knowledge.title: Correction to KNOWLEDGE-ca9ae048: the cause of the M15 token gap was not measured
knowledge.text: KNOWLEDGE-ca9ae048 says the Claude arm spends about 4.4 times the prompt tokens and about 4.1 times the cost because of its system prompt and tool preamble. The system prompt half is wrong and is withdrawn here. In evals/adr12/arms.py the method options_for builds ClaudeAgentOptions with tools, allowed_tools, permission_mode, setting_sources, cwd, model, max_turns, cli_path and env, and never sets system_prompt, so the Claude Code CLI receives that flag with an empty value and the arm runs with no system prompt of its own. Every measured fact in that record stands unchanged: 303691 prompt tokens against 69687, cost 0.3577 against 0.0871, median 3 turns against 2, median wall 6140 ms against 3723 ms, same model through the same gateway on one price list. What is withdrawn is the cause. M15 measured the gap and did not measure why it exists, and no cause should be read into these numbers. Candidate contributors, none of them isolated by this harness, are the CLI tool preamble and tool schemas, the scaffolding messages the CLI sends of its own accord, the extra turn in the median, and the framing asymmetry recorded beside this entry, in which this SDK arm receives a 251 character instruction to answer tersely from the files while the Claude arm receives none. Attributing the gap needs a controlled run that varies one contributor at a time. Raised by the independent L4 reviewer for M15 round 1 and confirmed in the source by the author.

knowledge.title: The ADR-12 harness frames the two arms differently and does not disclose it
knowledge.text: In evals/adr12/arms.py the ThisSdkArm passes a 251 character instruction which tells the model to answer questions about the files in its working folder, to answer with what the files say and nothing else, and to say plainly that it cannot do a thing rather than pretending it did. The ClaudeAgentSdkArm sets no system prompt at all, so the CLI runs with an empty one. FR-61 names only tools, permission mode, setting sources and env as the fields that must match between arms, so the harness meets the requirement as written, and the delivered report states no comparative verdict, so nothing published is false. The asymmetry is nonetheless undisclosed: it appears in neither the report Markdown, nor the report JSON metadata, nor the harness README, and no test pins either arm prompt. It plausibly moves the very measures under comparison, because an instruction to answer tersely pushes completion tokens and turns down. Before the comparison is run again, either give both arms the same instruction or record each arm prompt in the report metadata and pin both in the gate, and then say in the report which of the two was chosen. Raised by the independent L4 reviewer for M15 round 1 and confirmed in the source by the author. See KNOWLEDGE-eba388f8, which withdraws the causal claim this asymmetry undermines.

knowledge.title: M16 pre-flight: baseline, what M16 extends, and why the suite hung on 2026-09-16
knowledge.text: Baseline at b3654cf with no other python or node process: 1233 passed in 250.23 s, instrumented with a memory sampler every 2 s and a pytest faulthandler timeout of 120 s per test, with the owner working normally in parallel. Lowest free memory during the run was 924 MB of 16008, peak footprint of the whole suite 32 MB across at most 3 processes, and no test ran past 120 s. This refutes the diagnosis given during M15, which blamed memory pressure for two regression gate runs that hung: the suite passed today with less free memory than either hung run had. Memory pressure slows the suite, 250 s against 160 s, and does not hang it. The first hung run stopped at 35 percent, and tests 440 and 441 of 1233 are the two live gateway tests in test_golden_eval.py, the only place the suite waits on an outside server with no end to end deadline; this is the gap M15 measured, where the httpx 60 s timeout applies per read so a trickling response is never cut off. The second hung run position is unknown, because the author truncated its log when printing it. Code facts for M16: jsonschema 4.26.0 is already a runtime dependency used by the executor, so validating planner output adds nothing and NFR-21 holds. run_events.event_type carries no CHECK constraint, so the new event types need no migration. run_events.task_id exists, is unpopulated, and the schema comment reserves it for Phase 2, so a node id goes there per DECISION-8f8cc54c. The event sink is per run and owns sequence numbering, on both stores. Migrations are discovered by NNNN_lower_snake_case.sql name and checksummed, so M16 adds 0007. The AC-44 session guard in tests/conftest.py lists tracked tables in _TRACKED and skips a table a pending migration has not created, so M16 adds plan_versions and plan_node_states there.
